title: Meet A Practitioner And Trace A Path
objective: Meet arts practitioners through first-hand workshops or events, research arts organisations and education and career pathways, and summarise the influence in the pupil’s own words.

blocks.text: Silver · Unit 1 · Part 1D · Meet a practitioner and trace a path.
Part 1D joins a real meeting with research. Meet arts practitioners once a route is arranged. Gain first-hand experience of their work. Explore arts organisations and routes into learning and work.
Check PRACTITIONER_SLOT and ORG_SLOT with an adult. Empty or unconfirmed slots mean preparation. Reading a website or watching a recorded clip does not replace meeting a practitioner.
After the real activity and research, explain their influence on your thinking or arts practice. You can use speech, text, diagrams with labels or an exact scribe.

This deck directly evidences Silver Unit 1 Part 1D, Arts research. Source of award requirements: tools/artsaward/SPEC.json, Silver and universal rules. Silver is the Level 2 Award in the Arts, with TWO units evidenced separately. Mark parts P / A / N. ONE Attempted allowed PER UNIT. Any Not Attempted = Below Pass. Results are Pass / Below Pass only. The 20-file cap applies across the whole Silver portfolio, not per unit or lesson. Keep both units and all parts separately identifiable. Nine cumulative part files or two unit files with part sections are optional layouts, not award requirements. Every locator names the actual file plus page, slide or timecode. The four assessment areas are art form knowledge and understanding, creativity, planning and review, and communication. Only an adviser trained at Silver may assess. Delivery is through a validated centre; staff must confirm both conditions, which this deck does not assert are met. Advisers must not write plans, reviews or evidence for pupils. Read, prompt or scribe the pupil’s exact words and check them back without improving them. Core, Extend and Challenge vary support within Silver; each retains the full evidence meaning and the pupil’s own choices. Keep adult models and source quotations distinct from the pupil’s evidence. No forced private disclosure, public performance, filming or posting. Fourteen forty-minute lesson spines do not deliver the whole 95-hour programme; record actual additional guided and independent work.

Silver Unit 1 Part 1D requires meeting arts practitioners and gaining first-hand experience through workshops or events; research into arts organisations; education AND career pathways; and a summary in the pupil’s own words of the influence. Read both PRACTITIONER_SLOT and ORG_SLOT through the shared SLOTS.json reader. All current entries are empty; no person, organisation, date or booking is asserted. Support R1 pupils visit, R2 they come in or R3 live remote exchange. Before use, prepare checked primary information from the actual practitioner, arts organisation and education/training providers relevant to the pupil’s interests. Retain publisher, page title, public URL and section or pack page. Confirm availability and access rather than assuming a course or route suits every pupil. Do not invent a source pack as already prepared. Model and prepare through the first We Do, then pause for the real meeting and first-hand workshop/event in accurately recorded programme time. Resume with the actual findings. If not arranged, practise methods only and label all rehearsal; arrange actual contact and experience later. Research does not fabricate a meeting. For ORG_SLOT follow the actual live/active route and retain checked organisation research. A practitioner need not work for that organisation; do not invent a link. Staff may arrange access and record factual observations, not author the pupil’s account.

stages.title: Arrival · retrieve

blocks.text: Choose a question from your arts challenge that you could explore by watching, asking or trying a process.
Make it focused: How do you choose which print to keep? This asks about a decision you might test.
Keep the question and checked artist and organisation facts. Mark what still needs arranging. A question is preparation, not completed contact.
Choose support for taking part and recording: a reader, tool grip, thinking time or notes afterwards.

stages.data-ta1: Use the pupil’s actual challenge interests without supplying a topic for them. Read current slots. A question can be pointed to or dictated; preserve the pupil’s reason for choosing it.

stages.title: Starter · create the need

blocks.text: A biography can tell you about an artist’s work, but it cannot respond to your next question. During a live exchange, you can ask about a choice, watch a process and respond to what happens.

First-hand experience means being involved in the actual workshop or event. Follow the agreed activity and make a record of what you explored. Merely copying a fact about the person does not show that experience.
An arts organisation can support artists, present work or help people take part. Research the role of the actual organisation you explore. Do not assume its role from its name.
You will also examine education and career pathways. One asks how skills can be learnt; the other asks how people may use those skills in arts work.

stages.data-ta1: Keep the distinction between an actual encounter, participation and desk research clear. General possible organisation roles are questions to check, not claims about an unnamed local organisation.

stages.title: I Do · model

blocks.text: Watch how I prepare to learn from a process. I try tearing a paper strip quickly, then tear another while turning the paper slowly. I notice how the edges differ. This classroom model practises observation; it is not evidence of your practitioner meeting.
I form a question from what I saw: What helps you choose a rough or smooth edge? If the artist explains a choice, I can ask a further question linked to their answer.
During a real workshop, I follow the agreed activity and keep a sample or a located record of my action. I note who led it and what I tried. I record only what happened.

blocks.title: Learn from a real encounter
blocks.caption: An actual encounter gives you findings to reflect on.
blocks.alt: WATCH: notice a process choice. ASK: follow the actual answer. TRY: join the agreed activity. KEEP: record what happened. An actual encounter gives you findings to reflect on.

blocks.text: Afterwards, I separate their words from my own observations. A direct quote needs an accurate record. If I am unsure of the wording, I use a faithful summary and identify it as a summary.
I might want to change a method I use, or decide it does not suit my aim. Either influence needs a reason connected to something I genuinely learnt.

stages.data-ta1: Make the adult paper demonstration before pupil practice. Model asking and evidence capture without role-playing a fictional completed interview. Observe setting safety and consent rules for actual activities and records.

stages.title: We Do · everyone commits

data.heading: Keep the research strands distinct
data.instruction: Sort the five example records by their stated main purpose. These are record types, not facts about a named person or evidence that your own encounter happened.

items.label: A real workshop sample and note identify the practitioner, the meeting and the task I personally tried.
items.feedback: This can record a first-hand encounter when the named meeting and activity really occurred.

items.label: A checked arts-centre page explains its role and who can take part.
items.feedback: This answers an organisation question. It does not replace meeting a practitioner.

items.label: A provider’s current course page states skills taught and entry requirements.
items.feedback: This is an education route. Check the real source and access details before treating it as available.

items.label: A practitioner’s actual account describes an arts work role and the skills it involves.
items.feedback: This informs a career route, without guaranteeing work or earnings.

items.label: My own account explains how something I explored affects my next arts choice.
items.feedback: This records influence in the pupil’s own words, supported by a real finding.

data.discussion: Meet practitioners through the arranged first-hand workshop or event. Then check your real encounter, organisation, education and career sources. Explain the influence yourself and leave missing contact or research open.

stages.data-ta1: Read the actual prompt and choices; support the pupil to commit before checking. Use the item feedback as a model reason, not a judgement on personal taste. Keep real trials, meetings, views and project actions separate from these teaching examples.

stages.title: I Do 2 · connect

blocks.text: A pathway is a possible route, not a promise. I can trace learning into work while checking what each step needs. I need evidence for both sides of the route.

blocks.title: Check learning and work separately
blocks.caption: Use checked sources; a possible route is not a guarantee.
blocks.alt: EDUCATION ROUTE: skills and ways to learn, entry and access details. CAREER ROUTE: roles and kinds of work, skills and next steps. Use checked sources; a possible route is not a guarantee.

blocks.text: I show how to read the course page beside the artist or organisation source. I find what can be learnt, who the route is for and any stated entry steps. I keep the source title and exact location.
Then I find what an arts role involves. I separate a source fact from a guess about pay, access or success. If the page does not answer a question, I mark that gap for further checking.
Finally, I connect a finding to my interest: this route includes a skill I want to develop. The learner chooses that link; an adult cannot write the influence for them.

stages.data-ta1: Use the actual checked primary pages prepared for this group and read relevant text aloud. If absent, model only the questions and source fields; do not fill gaps with invented course or career facts.

stages.title: We Do 2 · lab

blocks.text: With a partner or adult, check a real finding from your encounter against its record. Does it identify who you met, what the activity was and what you personally explored?
Now check the organisation and pathway sources. Can you find an organisation role, an education route and a career route? Keep the publisher, page title and source location beside each finding.
Ask which claim is least clear. Decide whether to check the source, ask a further question or keep the gap open. A bold guess is still a guess.

stages.data-ta1: Use actual post-encounter records. For preparation pupils, check source fields and questions without asserting contact. Keep each source distinct and help locate missing information without authoring a pupil finding.

stages.title: Independent · evidence

blocks.text: Use the real meeting, first-hand activity and checked sources for your own account. What did you learn about the artist and organisation? Name an education route and a career route.
Summarise the influence in your own words. What has changed in your understanding, interest or next arts choice? Point to a real finding that explains the link.

items: Core: use selected source passages, prompts and exact scribing. Keep the real meeting and first-hand activity, organisation research, education and career routes, and your own influence summary.
Extend: organise the same encounter, organisation, both pathway areas and own influence summary with clear source and evidence locations.
Challenge: keep the same full evidence and compare two possible routes or findings. Explain which better fits your present arts interest and why.

blocks.text: Retain your original notes when you revise the account. Check any scribed words with the adult. Name any contact or research still to do; do not present practice as a real meeting.

stages.data-ta1: Every route retains all five evidence strands. Scribe verbatim only and read back for assent. No invented minimum number of sources, meetings or practitioners; retain the register’s required experience and research meaning.

stages.title: Exit · check the trail

blocks.text: Find your real meeting record and organisation research. Check both pathway areas and your own summary of their influence. Keep source facts separate from your views.
Save them under Silver Unit 1 Part 1D. Record the actual file name plus page, slide or timecode for each item. Keep source details and any image credits with the relevant finding.
Name a genuine gap if one remains. Otherwise, choose an idea from this work that you may use in your arts challenge. You decide whether to adopt it, adapt it or leave it aside.

stages.data-ta1: Check real contact and active-experience evidence, source locators and both pathway types. Keep Unit 1 distinct from Unit 2. Arrange missing work honestly; the file check alone does not complete 1D.

print.intro: Learn through a real practitioner meeting and first-hand activity. Research an arts organisation, education and career routes, then explain the influence in your own words.

tiers: Core: use source passages and access help; retain real contact and activity, organisation research, both pathway areas and your own influence summary.
Extend: organise the same full encounter, research and influence evidence with sources and exact locations.
Challenge: retain all the same evidence and compare routes or findings to explain which fits your arts interest.
checks: A real practitioner meeting and first-hand activity are evidenced, or clearly identified as pending.
I researched the actual arts organisation and kept its source.
I investigated education AND career pathways.
My own words explain the influence of actual findings.
